## Read-Only Kubernetes Security Assessment

All commands below inspect state only. Avoid retrieving Secret data or using mutation verbs such as `create`, `apply`, `patch`, `delete`, `edit`, `exec`, `cp`, or `port-forward`.

### 1. Establish scope and preserve context

- [ ] Record the cluster and identity being assessed.

```bash
kubectl config current-context
kubectl config view --minify
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl version
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl get nodes -o wide
```

- [ ] Record broad access available to the current identity.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i --list
kubectl auth can-i --list --namespace=default
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i impersonate users
kubectl auth can-i impersonate groups
kubectl auth can-i impersonate serviceaccounts
```

`kubectl auth can-i` submits non-persistent authorization reviews; it does not alter cluster resources.

### 2. RBAC reachability

- [ ] Inventory roles and bindings.

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide
kubectl get roles --all-namespaces
kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o wide
```

- [ ] Inspect rules and subject-to-role relationships.

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles -o yaml
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml
kubectl get roles --all-namespaces -o yaml
kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o yaml
```

- [ ] Look for bindings to high-privilege roles and broad groups.

```bash
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECT-KINDS:.subjects[*].kind,SUBJECTS:.subjects[*].name,GROUPS:.subjects[*].namespace'
kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE-KIND:.roleRef.kind,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECT-KINDS:.subjects[*].kind,SUBJECTS:.subjects[*].name'
```

Review especially:

- `cluster-admin` and wildcard rules.
- Bindings to `system:authenticated`, `system:unauthenticated`, or broad custom groups.
- Service accounts bound to cluster-wide roles.
- Permissions for `secrets`, `pods/exec`, `pods/attach`, `serviceaccounts/token`, `rolebindings`, `clusterrolebindings`, `impersonate`, or admission configuration.

- [ ] Test effective permissions for selected identities, when impersonation is authorized.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:SERVICE_ACCOUNT --namespace=NAMESPACE
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:SERVICE_ACCOUNT --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:SERVICE_ACCOUNT --namespace=NAMESPACE
kubectl auth can-i create serviceaccounts/token --as=system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:SERVICE_ACCOUNT --namespace=NAMESPACE
kubectl auth can-i impersonate users --as=system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:SERVICE_ACCOUNT
```

### 3. Service-account exposure

- [ ] Inventory service accounts without exposing token contents.

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces
kubectl get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,AUTOMOUNT:.automountServiceAccountToken,SECRETS:.secrets[*].name,IMAGE-PULL-SECRETS:.imagePullSecrets[*].name'
```

- [ ] Identify workloads using service accounts and token automount settings.

```bash
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,SERVICE-ACCOUNT:.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.automountServiceAccountToken,HOST-NETWORK:.spec.hostNetwork,NODE:.spec.nodeName'
kubectl get deployments --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE-ACCOUNT:.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.template.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'

kubectl get statefulsets --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE-ACCOUNT:.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.template.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'
kubectl get jobs --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE-ACCOUNT:.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.template.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'
kubectl get cronjobs --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE-ACCOUNT:.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'
```

- [ ] Inspect projected service-account-token volumes and legacy token Secret metadata.

```bash
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o yaml
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces --field-selector=type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE-ACCOUNT:.metadata.annotations.kubernetes\.io/service-account\.name,CREATED:.metadata.creationTimestamp'
```

Do not use `kubectl get secret ... -o yaml`, because it returns encoded credential material.

### 4. Workload `securityContext`

- [ ] Inventory pod-level controls.

```bash
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,RUN-AS-USER:.spec.securityContext.runAsUser,RUN-AS-NONROOT:.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot,SECCOMP:.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type,FS-GROUP:.spec.securityContext.fsGroup,HOST-PID:.spec.hostPID,HOST-IPC:.spec.hostIPC,HOST-NETWORK:.spec.hostNetwork'
```

- [ ] Inventory container-level controls.

```bash
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,CONTAINERS:.spec.containers[*].name,PRIVILEGED:.spec.containers[*].securityContext.privileged,ALLOW-PRIV-ESC:.spec.containers[*].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation,RUN-AS-NONROOT:.spec.containers[*].securityContext.runAsNonRoot,READONLY-ROOTFS:.spec.containers[*].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem,SECCOMP:.spec.containers[*].securityContext.seccompProfile.type,CAP-ADD:.spec.containers[*].securityContext.capabilities.add,CAP-DROP:.spec.containers[*].securityContext.capabilities.drop'
```

- [ ] Inspect init and ephemeral containers as well.

```bash
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,INIT-CONTAINERS:.spec.initContainers[*].name,INIT-PRIVILEGED:.spec.initContainers[*].securityContext.privileged,INIT-ALLOW-PRIV-ESC:.spec.initContainers[*].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation,EPHEMERAL-CONTAINERS:.spec.ephemeralContainers[*].name,EPHEMERAL-PRIVILEGED:.spec.ephemeralContainers[*].securityContext.privileged'
```

- [ ] Review host access and sensitive volume mounts.

```bash
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,HOST-PATHS:.spec.volumes[*].hostPath.path,CONTAINER-MOUNTS:.spec.containers[*].volumeMounts[*].mountPath'
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o yaml
```

Flag privileged containers, privilege escalation, root execution, missing seccomp, added capabilities, writable root filesystems, host namespaces, host paths, and broadly mounted credentials.

- [ ] Check namespace Pod Security Admission labels.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get namespaces -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,ENFORCE:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce,ENFORCE-VERSION:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce-version,AUDIT:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/audit,WARN:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/warn'
```

### 5. Network policies

- [ ] Inventory policies and inspect selectors, policy types, peers, ports, and IP blocks.

```bash
kubectl get networkpolicies --all-namespaces -o wide
kubectl get networkpolicies --all-namespaces -o yaml
```

- [ ] Compare policies with workload labels and pod IPs.

```bash
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --show-labels -o wide
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get services --all-namespaces -o wide
kubectl get endpointslices --all-namespaces
```

Check for:

- Namespaces with no policies.
- Missing default-deny ingress or egress coverage.
- Policies whose pod selectors match no workloads.
- Unrestricted `{}` peers or broad `ipBlock` CIDRs.
- Egress access to metadata services, control-plane endpoints, or arbitrary Internet destinations.
- Required DNS traffic being absent from egress rules.
- Assumptions unsupported by the installed CNI.

- [ ] Identify the networking implementation from system workloads.

```bash
kubectl get daemonsets --namespace=kube-system
kubectl get pods --namespace=kube-system -o wide
```

### 6. Audit evidence

- [ ] Record API events as supporting operational evidence.

```bash
kubectl get events --all-namespaces --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get events --all-namespaces -o yaml
```

Events are not a substitute for Kubernetes API audit logs and may have short retention.

- [ ] For self-managed control planes, inspect API-server audit configuration.

```bash
kubectl get pods --namespace=kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o wide
kubectl get pods --namespace=kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml
```

Review API-server arguments and mounts for:

- `--audit-policy-file`
- `--audit-log-path`
- `--audit-log-maxage`
- `--audit-log-maxbackup`
- `--audit-log-maxsize`

- [ ] Inspect accessible control-plane logs without modifying workloads.

kubectl logs --namespace=kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver --prefix=true --timestamps=true --since=24h
```

- [ ] Capture authorization denials and admission failures visible in events or API-server logs.

```bash
kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector=reason=FailedCreate
kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector=reason=FailedScheduling

### 7. Evidence handling

## Read-only Kubernetes cluster assessment

Replace `<namespace>`, `<service-account>`, and `<pod>` as needed. These commands only retrieve information or submit authorization-review queries. Avoid `apply`, `create`, `delete`, `edit`, `exec`, `patch`, `replace`, `rollout`, `scale`, and `set`.

### 1. Scope and cluster identity

- [ ] Confirm the current context before collecting evidence.

```bash
kubectl config current-context
kubectl config view --minify
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl version
kubectl api-resources
```

- [ ] Record namespace and node inventory.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
```

### 2. RBAC reachability

- [ ] Capture RBAC objects and subject mappings.

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide
kubectl get roles -A
kubectl get rolebindings -A -o wide
kubectl get clusterroles,clusterrolebindings,roles,rolebindings -A -o yaml
```

- [ ] Inspect bindings for privileged groups and service accounts.

```bash
kubectl describe clusterrolebindings
kubectl describe rolebindings -A
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml
kubectl get rolebindings -A -o yaml
```

Look for:

- `cluster-admin` or wildcard-bearing roles.
- Bindings to `system:authenticated`, `system:unauthenticated`, or broad identity-provider groups.
- Service accounts bound to cluster-wide roles.
- Permissions involving `secrets`, `pods/exec`, `pods/attach`, `serviceaccounts/token`, RBAC objects, admission configuration, or impersonation.
- Wildcards in `apiGroups`, `resources`, `verbs`, or `nonResourceURLs`.

- [ ] Determine the current identity's effective permissions.

```bash
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i --list
kubectl auth can-i --list --namespace=<namespace>
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*'
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create pods --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create serviceaccounts/token --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i impersonate users
kubectl auth can-i impersonate groups
kubectl auth can-i impersonate serviceaccounts
```

- [ ] If authorized to perform impersonation checks, assess a service account without obtaining or using its token.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> --namespace=<namespace>
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> --all-namespaces
```

Authorization checks may themselves appear in API audit records.

### 3. Service-account exposure

- [ ] Inventory service accounts and token automount settings.

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o yaml
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,AUTOMOUNT:.automountServiceAccountToken'
```

- [ ] Identify workload service-account assignments.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,SERVICE_ACCOUNT:.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A -o yaml
```

Check both the workload and service account for `automountServiceAccountToken`; workload-level settings take precedence.

- [ ] Inspect projected service-account token volumes.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
kubectl describe pods -A
```

Look for:

- `projected.serviceAccountToken`.
- Excessively long `expirationSeconds`.
- Broad or inappropriate token `audience`.
- Token mounts in containers that do not need Kubernetes API access.
- Shared service accounts used by unrelated workloads.
- Use of the namespace `default` service account.

- [ ] Identify legacy service-account token Secrets without printing secret data.

```bash
kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector=type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token
kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector=type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE_ACCOUNT:.metadata.annotations.kubernetes\.io/service-account\.name'
```

- [ ] Inspect pod references to Secrets and environment sources.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A -o yaml
```

Look for `secretKeyRef`, `envFrom.secretRef`, secret volumes, image pull secrets, and Secrets mounted into unnecessary sidecars. Avoid `kubectl get secret ... -o yaml/json`, which can expose credential values.

### 4. Workload `securityContext`

- [ ] Collect pod and controller specifications.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o wide
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A -o yaml
kubectl describe pods -A
```

- [ ] Review pod-level settings:

- `runAsNonRoot: true`
- Explicit non-zero `runAsUser` and `runAsGroup`
- Appropriate `fsGroup` and `fsGroupChangePolicy`
- `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`
- No unnecessary `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`, or `hostIPC`
- No unsafe `hostPath` volumes
- Appropriate supplemental groups

- [ ] Review every regular, init, and ephemeral container:

- `privileged` is absent or `false`
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` where practical
- `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`
- Only explicitly required capabilities are added
- No sensitive host device mounts
- Resource requests and limits are defined
- Images are pinned appropriately and avoid mutable tags where policy requires it

- [ ] Inspect runtime exposure and image details.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,HOST_NETWORK:.spec.hostNetwork,HOST_PID:.spec.hostPID,HOST_IPC:.spec.hostIPC'
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{"\t"}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{range .spec.containers[*]}{.name}{":"}{.image}{" "}{end}{"\n"}{end}'
```

- [ ] Check namespace Pod Security Admission labels.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get namespaces -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,ENFORCE:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce,ENFORCE_VERSION:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce-version,AUDIT:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/audit,WARN:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/warn'
```

### 5. Network policies

- [ ] Inventory all policies and their selectors.

```bash
kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o wide
kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o yaml
kubectl describe networkpolicies -A
```

- [ ] Compare policies with workloads and labels.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A --show-labels
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get services -A -o wide
kubectl get endpointslices -A
```

- [ ] For each namespace, verify:

- Every sensitive pod is selected by at least one relevant policy.
- Default-deny ingress and egress coverage exists where required.
- Required DNS egress remains explicit.
- Ingress sources use suitably narrow pod and namespace selectors.
- Egress destinations and ports are constrained.
- Empty selectors such as `{}` are intentional.
- `ipBlock` ranges are not unnecessarily broad.
- Exceptions do not permit unexpected cross-namespace access.
- Policies cover actual pod labels, not stale or mismatched selectors.

NetworkPolicy enforcement also depends on the installed CNI; the presence of policy objects alone does not prove enforcement.

### 6. Audit and supporting evidence

- [ ] Record recent API-related events.

```bash
kubectl get events -A
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get events -A -o yaml
```

Events are supporting evidence, not a substitute for Kubernetes API audit logs.

## Read-only Kubernetes cluster assessment

Replace `<namespace>`, `<service-account>`, and `<pod>` as needed. These commands only retrieve information or submit authorization-review queries. Avoid `apply`, `create`, `delete`, `edit`, `exec`, `patch`, `replace`, `rollout`, `scale`, and `set`.

### 1. Scope and cluster identity

- [ ] Confirm the current context before collecting evidence.

```bash
kubectl config current-context
kubectl config view --minify
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl version
kubectl api-resources
```

- [ ] Record namespace and node inventory.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
```

### 2. RBAC reachability

- [ ] Capture RBAC objects and subject mappings.

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide
kubectl get roles -A
kubectl get rolebindings -A -o wide
kubectl get clusterroles,clusterrolebindings,roles,rolebindings -A -o yaml
```

- [ ] Inspect bindings for privileged groups and service accounts.

```bash
kubectl describe clusterrolebindings
kubectl describe rolebindings -A
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml
kubectl get rolebindings -A -o yaml
```

Look for:

- `cluster-admin` or wildcard-bearing roles.
- Bindings to `system:authenticated`, `system:unauthenticated`, or broad identity-provider groups.
- Service accounts bound to cluster-wide roles.
- Permissions involving `secrets`, `pods/exec`, `pods/attach`, `serviceaccounts/token`, RBAC objects, admission configuration, or impersonation.
- Wildcards in `apiGroups`, `resources`, `verbs`, or `nonResourceURLs`.

- [ ] Determine the current identity's effective permissions.

```bash
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i --list
kubectl auth can-i --list --namespace=<namespace>
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*'
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create pods --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create serviceaccounts/token --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i impersonate users
kubectl auth can-i impersonate groups
kubectl auth can-i impersonate serviceaccounts
```

- [ ] If authorized to perform impersonation checks, assess a service account without obtaining or using its token.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> --namespace=<namespace>
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> --all-namespaces
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> --all-namespaces
```

Authorization checks may themselves appear in API audit records.

### 3. Service-account exposure

- [ ] Inventory service accounts and token automount settings.

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o yaml
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,AUTOMOUNT:.automountServiceAccountToken'
```

- [ ] Identify workload service-account assignments.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,SERVICE_ACCOUNT:.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A -o yaml
```

Check both the workload and service account for `automountServiceAccountToken`; workload-level settings take precedence.

- [ ] Inspect projected service-account token volumes.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
kubectl describe pods -A
```

Look for:

- `projected.serviceAccountToken`.
- Excessively long `expirationSeconds`.
- Broad or inappropriate token `audience`.
- Token mounts in containers that do not need Kubernetes API access.
- Shared service accounts used by unrelated workloads.
- Use of the namespace `default` service account.

- [ ] Identify legacy service-account token Secrets without printing secret data.

```bash
kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector=type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token
kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector=type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE_ACCOUNT:.metadata.annotations.kubernetes\.io/service-account\.name'
```

- [ ] Inspect pod references to Secrets and environment sources.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A -o yaml
```

Look for `secretKeyRef`, `envFrom.secretRef`, secret volumes, image pull secrets, and Secrets mounted into unnecessary sidecars. Avoid `kubectl get secret ... -o yaml/json`, which can expose credential values.

### 4. Workload `securityContext`

- [ ] Collect pod and controller specifications.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o wide
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A -o yaml
kubectl describe pods -A
```

- [ ] Review pod-level settings:

- `runAsNonRoot: true`
- Explicit non-zero `runAsUser` and `runAsGroup`
- Appropriate `fsGroup` and `fsGroupChangePolicy`
- `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`
- No unnecessary `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`, or `hostIPC`
- No unsafe `hostPath` volumes
- Appropriate supplemental groups

- [ ] Review every regular, init, and ephemeral container:

- `privileged` is absent or `false`
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` where practical
- `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`
- Only explicitly required capabilities are added
- No sensitive host device mounts
- Resource requests and limits are defined
- Images are pinned appropriately and avoid mutable tags where policy requires it

- [ ] Inspect runtime exposure and image details.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,HOST_NETWORK:.spec.hostNetwork,HOST_PID:.spec.hostPID,HOST_IPC:.spec.hostIPC'
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{"\t"}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{range .spec.containers[*]}{.name}{":"}{.image}{" "}{end}{"\n"}{end}'
```

- [ ] Check namespace Pod Security Admission labels.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get namespaces -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,ENFORCE:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce,ENFORCE_VERSION:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce-version,AUDIT:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/audit,WARN:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/warn'
```

### 5. Network policies

- [ ] Inventory all policies and their selectors.

```bash
kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o wide
kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o yaml
kubectl describe networkpolicies -A
```

- [ ] Compare policies with workloads and labels.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A --show-labels
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get services -A -o wide
kubectl get endpointslices -A
```

- [ ] For each namespace, verify:

- Every sensitive pod is selected by at least one relevant policy.
- Default-deny ingress and egress coverage exists where required.
- Required DNS egress remains explicit.
- Ingress sources use suitably narrow pod and namespace selectors.
- Egress destinations and ports are constrained.
- Empty selectors such as `{}` are intentional.
- `ipBlock` ranges are not unnecessarily broad.
- Exceptions do not permit unexpected cross-namespace access.
- Policies cover actual pod labels, not stale or mismatched selectors.

NetworkPolicy enforcement also depends on the installed CNI; the presence of policy objects alone does not prove enforcement.

### 6. Audit and supporting evidence

- [ ] Record recent API-related events.

```bash
kubectl get events -A
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get events -A -o yaml
```

Events are supporting evidence, not a substitute for Kubernetes API audit logs.

- [ ] Inspect control-plane component configuration when exposed as Kubernetes resources.

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o yaml
kubectl get configmaps -n kube-system
kubectl describe configmaps -n kube-system
```

For self-managed control planes, inspect the API server pod specification for:

- `--audit-policy-file`
- `--audit-log-path`
- `--audit-log-maxage`
- `--audit-log-maxbackup`
- `--audit-log-maxsize`
- Audit webhook configuration
- Mounted audit-policy and log paths

- [ ] Where permitted, inspect API server logs without entering containers.

```bash
kubectl logs -n kube-system <kube-apiserver-pod> --timestamps
kubectl logs -n kube-system <kube-apiserver-pod> --previous --timestamps
```

Managed Kubernetes services commonly deliver audit logs to provider logging rather than pod logs. Document the provider log source, retention, access controls, and time range separately.

- [ ] Preserve assessment metadata in notes:

- Context, cluster endpoint, and Kubernetes version
- Assessor identity from `kubectl auth whoami`
- UTC collection time
- Commands executed
- Namespace and resource scope
- Authorization failures or inaccessible evidence
- Output files and cryptographic hashes, if evidence is exported

## Read-Only Kubernetes Cluster Assessment

All commands below are inspection-only. Avoid `kubectl edit`, `apply`, `patch`, `replace`, `delete`, `create`, `exec`, `cp`, `port-forward`, and secret-value retrieval.

### 1. Establish scope and evidence context

- [ ] Confirm the target cluster and client/server versions.

```bash
kubectl config current-context
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl version
kubectl get --raw='/version'
kubectl get namespaces -o wide
```

- [ ] Record node and workload inventory.

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -A -o wide
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A
```

### 2. RBAC reachability

- [ ] Review the current identity's effective permissions.

```bash
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i --list
kubectl auth can-i --list -A
```

- [ ] Check sensitive capabilities explicitly.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -A
kubectl auth can-i create pods -A
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -A
kubectl auth can-i impersonate users
kubectl auth can-i impersonate groups
kubectl auth can-i bind clusterroles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io
kubectl auth can-i escalate clusterroles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

- [ ] Inventory roles and bindings.

```bash
kubectl get roles,rolebindings -A -o wide
kubectl get clusterroles,clusterrolebindings -o wide
kubectl get rolebindings -A -o yaml
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml
```

- [ ] Review powerful or broadly scoped rules.

```bash
kubectl describe clusterrole cluster-admin
kubectl get clusterroles -o yaml
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml
```

Look for:

- Wildcards in `apiGroups`, `resources`, or `verbs`
- Access to secrets, token requests, pod creation, `pods/exec`, or `pods/attach`
- RBAC `bind`, `escalate`, or `impersonate`
- Bindings to `system:authenticated`, `system:unauthenticated`, or broad groups
- Namespace roles bound to unexpected users, groups, or service accounts
- Aggregated ClusterRoles and unexpected `aggregate-to-*` labels

- [ ] If authorized to impersonate service accounts, test effective access without using their credentials.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> --list -n <namespace>
kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> get secrets -n <namespace>
kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account> create pods -n <namespace>
```

### 3. Service-account exposure

- [ ] Inventory service accounts and their configured pull secrets.

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o wide
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o yaml
```

- [ ] Identify workloads using default or privileged service accounts.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,SERVICE_ACCOUNT:.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,TYPE:.kind,NAME:.metadata.name,SERVICE_ACCOUNT:.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.template.spec.automountServiceAccountToken'
```

- [ ] Inspect projected token mounts without reading token contents.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <namespace>
```

Look for:

- Use of the `default` service account
- Missing or `true` `automountServiceAccountToken`
- Projected `serviceAccountToken` volumes
- Long token expiration settings or unexpected audiences
- Token-bearing volumes mounted into unnecessary containers
- Service accounts bound to cluster-wide roles
- Image pull secrets reused as general workload credentials

- [ ] Inventory secret metadata only. Do not request secret YAML or decoded data.

```bash
kubectl get secrets -A
kubectl get secrets -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,TYPE:.type,CREATED:.metadata.creationTimestamp'
```

### 4. Workload `securityContext`

- [ ] Capture pod-level security settings.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,HOST_NETWORK:.spec.hostNetwork,HOST_PID:.spec.hostPID,HOST_IPC:.spec.hostIPC,RUN_AS_USER:.spec.securityContext.runAsUser,RUN_AS_NON_ROOT:.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot,SECCOMP:.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type'
```

- [ ] Inspect complete workload templates and all container types.

```bash
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs -A -o yaml
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml
```

- [ ] Check individual high-risk workloads.

```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <namespace>
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <namespace> -o yaml
```

Look for:

- `privileged: true`
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation` absent or `true`
- Containers running as UID 0
- `runAsNonRoot` absent or `false`
- Writable root filesystems
- Added Linux capabilities, especially `SYS_ADMIN`, `NET_ADMIN`, or `SYS_PTRACE`
- Missing capability drop of `ALL`
- `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`, or `hostIPC`
- `hostPath` volumes, especially `/`, runtime sockets, `/proc`, or `/sys`
- Missing `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost` seccomp profiles
- Unconfined AppArmor or SELinux configuration
- Unsafe sysctls
- Elevated init or ephemeral containers
- Sensitive device mounts

- [ ] Review Pod Security Admission namespace labels.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
kubectl get namespaces -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,ENFORCE:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce,ENFORCE_VERSION:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/enforce-version,AUDIT:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/audit,WARN:.metadata.labels.pod-security\.kubernetes\.io/warn'
```

### 5. Network policies

- [ ] Inventory all policies and namespaces with no visible policy objects.

```bash
kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o wide
kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o yaml
kubectl describe networkpolicy -A
```

- [ ] Compare policy selectors with workload labels.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A --show-labels
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
```

For each namespace, verify:

- At least one policy selects intended workloads
- Default-deny ingress exists where required
- Default-deny egress exists where required
- DNS egress remains intentionally available
- Ingress and egress `policyTypes` are explicit
- Empty selectors are intentional
- Namespace and pod selectors do not accidentally broaden access
- `ipBlock` ranges and exclusions are justified
- Control-plane, metadata-service, and external egress are restricted as intended
- The installed CNI actually enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy

Note: A NetworkPolicy object does not prove enforcement. CNI configuration and traffic testing require separate validation.

### 6. Audit configuration and evidence

- [ ] Determine whether API-server audit flags are visible.

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml
kubectl describe pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver
```

Look for:

- `--audit-policy-file`
- `--audit-log-path`
- `--audit-webhook-config-file`
- Audit log rotation and retention flags
- Mounted audit-policy and audit-log paths

- [ ] Inspect the referenced audit policy if it is exposed as a non-secret Kubernetes object.

```bash
kubectl get configmaps -n kube-system
kubectl get configmap <audit-policy-configmap> -n kube-system -o yaml
```

- [ ] Review API-server logs only where audit events are intentionally emitted there.

```bash
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver --all-containers=true --since=1h
```

- [ ] Collect supplementary event evidence. Kubernetes Events are not a substitute for audit logs.

```bash
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get events -A -o yaml
```

Verify audit evidence covers:

- Authentication identity and impersonation
- Request verb, resource, namespace, and object name
- Authorization outcome and response status
- RBAC and workload changes
- Secret access without recording secret values
- Pod `exec`, `attach`, and port-forward activity
- Audit destination health, retention, integrity, and access controls

On managed Kubernetes, control-plane audit logs may exist only in the provider logging service and may not be accessible through `kubectl`. Record that limitation rather than treating absent API-server pods or logs as proof that auditing is disabled.

- [ ] Determine whether API-server audit flags are visible.

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml
kubectl describe pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver
```

Look for:

- `--audit-policy-file`
- `--audit-log-path`
- `--audit-webhook-config-file`
- Audit log rotation and retention flags
- Mounted audit-policy and audit-log paths

- [ ] Inspect the referenced audit policy if it is exposed as a non-secret Kubernetes object.

```bash
kubectl get configmaps -n kube-system
kubectl get configmap <audit-policy-configmap> -n kube-system -o yaml
```

- [ ] Review API-server logs only where audit events are intentionally emitted there.

```bash
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver --all-containers=true --since=1h
```

- [ ] Collect supplementary event evidence. Kubernetes Events are not a substitute for audit logs.

```bash
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get events -A -o yaml
```

Verify audit evidence covers:

- Authentication identity and impersonation
- Request verb, resource, namespace, and object name
- Authorization outcome and response status
- RBAC and workload changes
- Secret access without recording secret values
- Pod `exec`, `attach`, and port-forward activity
- Audit destination health, retention, integrity, and access controls

On managed Kubernetes, control-plane audit logs may exist only in the provider logging service and may not be accessible through `kubectl`. Record that limitation rather than treating absent API-server pods or logs as proof that auditing is disabled.

**Bounded Lab Workflow**

Assume `hashes.txt` contains only synthetic SHA-256 hashes. Hashcat mode `1400` is used as an example; verify the mode rather than guessing.

```bash
mkdir -p lab-audit
cd lab-audit

printf '%s\n' \
  'TrainingOnly1!' \
  'LabPassword2026!' \
  'Synthetic-Example-42' \
  'CorrectHorseLab7!' \
  'NeverUseInProduction!' \
  > lab-wordlist.txt
```

Identify or confirm the hash format:

```bash
hashcat --identify hashes.txt
hashcat --example-hashes -m 1400
```

Run a dictionary-only attack with a named session, dedicated potfile, periodic restore state, and a 15-minute limit:

```bash
hashcat \
  --session=training-lab-sha256 \
  --attack-mode=0 \
  --hash-type=1400 \
  --runtime=900 \
  --restore-timer=60 \
  --status \
  --status-timer=30 \
  --potfile-path=training-lab.potfile \
  hashes.txt \
  lab-wordlist.txt
```

If interrupted or stopped by the runtime bound, inspect the session:

```bash
hashcat --session=training-lab-sha256 --restore --restore-disable
```

For a normal continuation instead, omit `--restore-disable`:

```bash
hashcat --session=training-lab-sha256 --restore
```

Stop safely with `q` from Hashcat's interactive status prompt when possible. A completed or exhausted session may remove its restore file, in which case there is nothing left to resume.

Generate reports without displaying results directly in terminal history:

```bash
hashcat \
  --hash-type=1400 \
  --potfile-path=training-lab.potfile \
  --show \
  --outfile=cracked-report.txt \
  --outfile-format=1,2 \
  hashes.txt

hashcat \
  --hash-type=1400 \
  --potfile-path=training-lab.potfile \
  --left \
  --outfile=uncracked-report.txt \
  hashes.txt
```

Record the hash mode, session name, wordlist checksum, runtime limit, Hashcat version, cracked count, and uncracked count in the audit notes:

```bash
shasum -a 256 lab-wordlist.txt
hashcat --version
wc -l hashes.txt cracked-report.txt uncracked-report.txt
```

Treat `training-lab.potfile` and `cracked-report.txt` as sensitive lab artifacts and delete or archive them according to the lab's retention policy.

## Safe C2 Reference Architecture

Use an isolated, allowlisted environment with written authorization, fixed test windows, predefined source/destination ranges, and an emergency shutdown procedure.

```text
Authorized test hosts
  -> TLS redirector / policy gateway
  -> C2 control service
  -> task approval queue
  -> authenticated operator console

All components
  -> immutable audit store
  -> blue-team SIEM / EDR / network telemetry
```

### Redirector

- Expose only the redirector to test hosts; keep the control service on a private network.
- Permit only registered test assets, approved protocols, destinations, and exercise times.
- Apply rate limits, request-size limits, and immediate deny/revocation controls.
- Do not imitate unrelated third parties or conceal traffic from defenders.
- Treat it as a policy-enforcement gateway, not merely a traffic relay.

### Beacon Check-In

- Use a simple, documented periodic check-in from an approved test agent.
- Assign each asset a unique, revocable identity linked to the exercise inventory.
- Keep task types narrow and pre-approved; prohibit arbitrary command execution where possible.
- Enforce server-side expiration, maximum check-in frequency, task timeouts, and a global kill switch.
- Make traffic deliberately attributable through dedicated domains, certificates, headers, or test identifiers shared with exercise control.

### Mutual TLS

- Use an exercise-specific private CA, with separate client certificates for every agent and service.
- Validate both certificate chains and expected identities; do not rely solely on encryption.
- Use short-lived certificates, protected private keys, explicit revocation, and rotation procedures.
- Separate redirector-to-agent and redirector-to-control trust domains when practical.
- Log certificate identity, validation outcome, issuance, rotation, and revocation events without logging private keys.

### Operator Authentication

- Require centralized SSO, phishing-resistant MFA, and named individual accounts.
- Apply least-privilege roles such as observer, operator, approver, and administrator.
- Require dual approval for high-impact actions and scope changes.
- Use short sessions, reauthentication for sensitive actions, and rapid account revocation.
- Disallow shared accounts and record who requested, approved, modified, and executed each task.

### Audit Logging

- Record operator identity, agent identity, timestamps, task request and approval, execution result, configuration changes, and policy denials.
- Use synchronized clocks, append-only or immutable storage, integrity verification, encryption, and defined retention.
- Redact credentials, private keys, tokens, and unnecessary sensitive output.
- Send logs out of band so an unavailable C2 service cannot erase the audit trail.
- Give exercise control and designated defenders read access during the tabletop.

### Blue-Team Telemetry

Provide defenders with intentional visibility into:

- DNS queries and TLS connection metadata.
- Redirector access, policy-denial, and rate-limit logs.
- Certificate subjects, serials, fingerprints, and revocation events.
- EDR process and network events from test agents.
- Authentication, authorization, approval, and operator-session records.
- Correlation identifiers connecting an operator action to a task, check-in, and endpoint result.

Define expected detections before the exercise, including certificate anomalies, periodic connections, unauthorized assets, out-of-window activity, excessive tasking, and attempted policy bypasses. Decide in advance which indicators are disclosed immediately and which are revealed during debrief.

### Safety Controls

- Hard allowlists for agents, operators, networks, and task types.
- Automatic shutdown at exercise end.
- Per-agent and global revocation.
- Rate and concurrency limits.
- Independent monitoring by exercise control.
- Tested stop phrase and out-of-band communication channel.
- Data minimization and rules for handling accidental production data.
- Post-exercise certificate revocation, account disablement, log preservation, and infrastructure teardown.

For a tabletop, represent these components with diagrams and simulated events rather than operational implants or internet-accessible infrastructure.

## Safe Tabletop C2 Architecture

Use a **closed, non-production simulation environment** with synthetic beacons, allowlisted infrastructure, and documented rules of engagement.

### Core Components

- **Redirector**
  - Public-facing gateway that is the only component exposed to the exercise network.
  - Accepts traffic only from explicitly allowlisted source ranges or enrolled clients.
  - Performs rate limiting, basic protocol validation, and connection logging.
  - Forwards approved traffic to the internal C2 service without exposing its address.
  - Has no operator interface or long-term sensitive data.

- **Beacon check-in**
  - Simulated agents periodically request a task and submit synthetic status data.
  - Each beacon has a unique, short-lived identity tied to an approved exercise asset.
  - The server enforces expiration, revocation, payload limits, and strict task allowlists.
  - Check-ins should use predictable exercise windows rather than stealth-oriented timing.
  - Include a central kill switch that immediately disables tasking and rejects further check-ins.

- **Mutual TLS**
  - Both beacon and server authenticate with certificates issued by an exercise-specific private CA.
  - Certificates should be short-lived, uniquely assigned, and revocable.
  - Private keys should be stored in an approved secrets system or protected platform keystore.
  - The redirector should preserve authenticated identity to the internal service through a trusted mechanism.
  - Do not share certificates across systems or reuse production trust roots.

- **Operator authentication**
  - Place the operator console behind an identity-aware access gateway or VPN.
  - Require SSO, phishing-resistant MFA, role-based authorization, and time-limited sessions.
  - Separate roles such as exercise controller, operator, observer, and auditor.
  - Require dual approval for high-impact simulated actions.
  - Disable generic and shared operator accounts.

- **Audit logging**
  - Record authentication attempts, certificate issuance and revocation, beacon enrollment, check-ins, task creation, approvals, task delivery, results, configuration changes, and kill-switch use.
  - Include timestamp, actor, role, source, target asset, request ID, and exercise authorization reference.
  - Send logs to append-only or tamper-evident storage outside the C2 environment.
  - Never log private keys, authentication tokens, or unnecessary sensitive payload contents.

- **Blue-team telemetry**
  - Mirror relevant redirector, DNS, firewall, proxy, endpoint, identity, and application logs to defenders.
  - Tag exercise traffic so controllers can distinguish it from an actual compromise while preserving realistic detections.
  - Provide expected indicators and asset scope to a trusted control-cell contact, not necessarily all defenders during a blind phase.
  - Define escalation paths for unexpected hosts, out-of-scope traffic, certificate misuse, or signs of a real intrusion.
  - Measure alert generation, triage time, correlation quality, containment decisions, and false positives.

### Conceptual Flow

```text
Synthetic beacon
  -> allowlisted exercise network
  -> redirector and mTLS validation
  -> internal C2 task broker
  -> approved task allowlist

Operator
  -> identity gateway, SSO, and MFA
  -> role and approval checks
  -> task broker

All components
  -> centralized tamper-evident audit store
  -> blue-team SIEM and exercise control cell
```

### Safety Boundaries

- Keep the environment isolated from production and the public internet where practical.
- Use only pre-enrolled assets and non-sensitive test data.
- Constrain tasking to harmless simulations, such as reporting a marker file or returning synthetic inventory.
- Enforce network egress restrictions at infrastructure controls, not merely by policy.
- Predefine stop conditions, emergency contacts, certificate revocation, data-retention periods, and cleanup validation.
- Treat traffic from unknown systems as a possible real incident, not automatically as part of the exercise.

**Safe C2 Reference Architecture**

```text
Authorized test hosts
  |
  | HTTPS with mutual TLS
  v
Internet-facing redirector
  |
  | Allowlisted, authenticated relay
  v
Isolated C2 service
  |
  +--> Append-only audit store / SIEM
  |
  +--> Operator access gateway
          |
          +--> SSO + MFA + RBAC
```

**Redirector**

- Treat it as a narrow reverse proxy, not a command server.
- Place it in a dedicated test account, network, and domain.
- Accept traffic only during approved exercise windows and from registered test identities where feasible.
- Forward only the expected protocol and paths to the internal C2 service.
- Apply rate limits, request-size limits, health monitoring, and an emergency shutdown control.
- Do not retain payloads or operator credentials on the redirector.

**Beacon check-in**

- Use predictable, documented intervals with bounded jitter for load testing, not stealth.
- Keep messages minimal: exercise identifier, pseudonymous host identifier, timestamp, status, and task/result references.
- Enforce task expiration, maximum execution counts, message-size limits, and explicit host enrollment.
- Restrict commands to a preapproved tabletop action catalog. Avoid arbitrary shell execution.
- Provide a global kill switch and automatic expiration at the end of the engagement.

**Mutual TLS**

- Use a private exercise CA with separate client identities for each enrolled test host.
- Validate both server and client certificates; do not disable hostname or chain verification.
- Use short-lived certificates, protect private keys, and support immediate revocation.
- Separate redirector-to-C2 credentials from beacon-to-redirector credentials.
- Pin trust to the exercise CA where operationally appropriate, rather than bypassing normal TLS controls.

**Operator authentication**

- Require access through an identity-aware gateway or VPN.
- Use organizational SSO, phishing-resistant MFA, and role-based access control.
- Separate roles such as exercise lead, operator, observer, and auditor.
- Require approval for high-impact simulated actions using a two-person rule.
- Use short sessions, no shared accounts, and managed operator workstations.

- Authentication successes and failures.

- Build dashboards for check-in volume, target scope, operator actions, certificate failures, and policy violations.
- Establish escalation paths for unexpected targets, excessive traffic, real compromise indicators, or activity outside the approved window.
- Preserve enough telemetry for after-action detection validation without exposing sensitive payload content.

- Written scope, target allowlist, prohibited actions, and data-handling rules.
- Network-level enforcement of scope, not merely operator instructions.

- Tested stop procedure with named contacts available throughout the exercise.
- Post-exercise certificate revocation, account removal, log preservation, and infrastructure destruction.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Sequential SSH credential-test harness for an isolated loopback lab."""

import argparse
import ipaddress
import socket
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

import paramiko


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Account:
    username: str
    password: str


# Fixed synthetic test accounts.
ACCOUNTS = (
    Account("synthetic_alpha", "LabOnly-Alpha-01!"),
    Account("synthetic_bravo", "LabOnly-Bravo-02!"),
    Account("synthetic_charlie", "LabOnly-Charlie-03!"),
    Account("synthetic_delta", "LabOnly-Delta-04!"),
    Account("synthetic_echo", "LabOnly-Echo-05!"),
)

LOCKOUT_MARKERS = (
    "locked out",
    "lockout",
    "account locked",
    "too many authentication failures",
    "too many failed",
    "temporarily disabled",
    "temporarily locked",
    "maximum authentication attempts",
)


def require_loopback(host: str) -> str:
    """Accept only literal loopback addresses, avoiding DNS rebinding."""
    try:
        address = ipaddress.ip_address(host)
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(
            "host must be a literal loopback IP such as 127.0.0.1 or ::1"
        ) from exc

    if not address.is_loopback:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("refusing non-loopback SSH host")

    return str(address)

    results = socket.getaddrinfo(
        host,

        family=socket.AF_UNSPEC,
        type=socket.SOCK_STREAM,
    )
    if not results:
        raise ValueError("host did not resolve")

    endpoints: list[tuple[int, tuple]] = []
    seen: set[tuple[int, tuple]] = set()

    for family, socktype, proto, _canonname, sockaddr in results:
        address = ipaddress.ip_address(sockaddr[0])
        if not address.is_loopback:
            raise ValueError(
                f"refusing non-loopback resolution: {host!r} resolved to {address}"
            )

        endpoint = (family, sockaddr)
        if endpoint not in seen:
            seen.add(endpoint)
            endpoints.append(endpoint)

    return endpoints

    if text is None:
        return None

    if isinstance(text, bytes):

    folded = rendered.casefold()
    if any(marker in folded for marker in LOCKOUT_MARKERS):

    return None

    endpoint: tuple[int, tuple],

) -> tuple[str, Optional[str]]:

        return "rejected", None

    transport: Optional[paramiko.Transport] = None

    try:
        sock = socket.socket(family, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        sock.settimeout(CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)
        sock.connect(sockaddr)

        transport = paramiko.Transport(sock)
        transport.banner_timeout = CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS
        transport.auth_timeout = CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS
        transport.start_client(timeout=CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)

        banner = lockout_text(transport.remote_version)
        if banner:
            return "lockout", banner

        # fallback=False prevents an additional keyboard-interactive attempt.
        transport.auth_password(username, password, fallback=False)

        banner = lockout_text(transport.get_banner())
        if banner:
            return "lockout", banner

        return ("accepted", None) if transport.is_authenticated() else ("rejected", None)

    except paramiko.AuthenticationException as exc:
        if transport is not None:
            banner = lockout_text(transport.get_banner())
            if banner:
                return "lockout", banner

        banner = lockout_text(exc)
        if banner:
            return "lockout", banner
        return "rejected", None

    except (paramiko.SSHException, OSError, EOFError) as exc:
        if transport is not None:
            banner = lockout_text(transport.get_banner())
            if banner:
                return "lockout", banner

        banner = lockout_text(exc)
        if banner:
            return "lockout", banner
        return "error", str(exc)

    finally:
        if transport is not None:
            transport.close()
        elif sock is not None:
            sock.close()


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Test five fixed synthetic SSH accounts sequentially."
    )
    parser.add_argument("host", help="must resolve exclusively to loopback addresses")
    parser.add_argument("--port", type=int, default=22)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if not 1 <= args.port <= 65535:
        parser.error("--port must be between 1 and 65535")

    try:
        endpoints = resolve_loopback(args.host, args.port)
    except (ValueError, OSError) as exc:
        parser.error(str(exc))

    # Connect to the already validated numeric endpoint, avoiding a second DNS lookup.
    endpoint = endpoints[0]

    for index, (username, password) in enumerate(ACCOUNTS):
        status, detail = attempt(endpoint, username, password)
        print(f"{username}: {status}", flush=True)

        if status == "lockout":
            print(f"Stopping on lockout banner: {detail}", flush=True)
            return 2

        if status == "error" and detail:
            print(f"  Error: {detail}", flush=True)

        if index < len(ACCOUNTS) - 1:
            time.sleep(DELAY_SECONDS)

    return 0

# Incident Post-Mortem: Malicious OAuth Application

## Incident Summary

On [date], the security team identified unauthorized access to employee accounts associated with a malicious third-party OAuth application. The application requested permissions that enabled it to access account data without requiring continued use of the affected users’ passwords.

The incident was contained by revoking the application’s OAuth grants, disabling affected sessions, and resetting credentials where appropriate. This post-mortem documents the current understanding of the incident and focuses on improving organizational controls rather than assigning individual blame.

## Timeline

- **[Date/time]:** Malicious OAuth application was authorized by one or more employees.
- **[Date/time]:** The application began accessing authorized account data.
- **[Date/time]:** Suspicious activity was detected through [security alert/user report/audit review].
- **[Date/time]:** Security initiated incident response and identified the associated OAuth application.
- **[Date/time]:** New authorizations for the application were blocked.
- **[Date/time]:** Existing OAuth grants and active sessions were revoked.
- **[Date/time]:** Affected users and relevant stakeholders were notified.
- **[Date/time]:** Investigation confirmed the known scope of accessed accounts and data.
- **[Date/time]:** Recovery actions were completed, and enhanced monitoring was established.

## Root Cause

The immediate cause was authorization of a malicious OAuth application that presented itself as a legitimate service. Once approved, the application received valid OAuth tokens and used the permissions granted to access account resources.

Contributing factors included:

- Users could authorize third-party applications without prior administrative approval.
- The application requested permissions that were broader than required for its stated function.
- Existing controls placed insufficient emphasis on OAuth consent phishing.
- Monitoring did not immediately distinguish malicious token use from legitimate application activity.
- OAuth grants were not subject to sufficiently frequent review or automated risk-based revocation.

No single action or individual caused the incident. The event resulted from a combination of deceptive attacker behavior and gaps in technical and procedural controls.

## Impact

- **Accounts affected:** [number or range]
- **Data potentially accessed:** [email, files, contacts, profile data, or other resources]
- **Confirmed data exfiltration:** [summary or “not confirmed”]
- **Operational impact:** [service disruption, account lockouts, investigation effort]
- **External impact:** [customers, partners, or “none identified”]
- **Duration:** From approximately [time] to [time]

The investigation found [no evidence/evidence] that passwords were directly exposed. However, OAuth tokens allowed access within the permissions granted to the application. The impact assessment remains subject to revision if additional evidence becomes available.

## Remediation

Completed actions:

- Revoked all OAuth grants associated with the malicious application.
- Blocked the application and related identifiers across the environment.
- Invalidated affected sessions and tokens.
- Reset credentials and reviewed multifactor authentication settings for affected accounts.
- Reviewed audit logs for suspicious access, persistence, and data transfer.
- Notified affected users and relevant internal stakeholders.
- Added indicators associated with the campaign to security monitoring.

Planned actions:

- Restrict OAuth application consent to approved or verified publishers.
- Require administrative approval for applications requesting sensitive permissions.
- Implement automated detection for unusual OAuth grants and token activity.
- Establish recurring reviews of third-party application access.
- Improve logging, alerting, and retention for OAuth consent and API activity.
- Update phishing training to include OAuth consent and token-based attacks.
- Test OAuth application revocation procedures during future incident-response exercises.

## Lessons Learned

- Strong password and multifactor authentication controls do not fully prevent OAuth consent phishing.
- OAuth permissions and tokens should be treated as sensitive credentials.
- Consent policies should apply least-privilege principles and default to administrative review for high-risk access.
- Detection must cover application authorization and token behavior, not only interactive sign-ins.
- Centralized visibility into third-party applications is necessary for timely investigation and containment.
- Clear revocation procedures reduced containment time and should be documented and exercised regularly.
- Security awareness guidance should help users evaluate application identity, requested permissions, and business need before granting access.

# Incident Post-Mortem: Malicious OAuth Application

## Incident Summary

On **[date]**, the security team identified a malicious third-party OAuth application that had obtained access to **[affected service/environment]** through user consent. The application requested permissions that allowed it to access **[mail, files, profile data, or other resources]** without collecting users’ passwords directly.

After discovery, we disabled the application, revoked associated OAuth grants and sessions, contained affected accounts, and began an investigation. This incident was resolved on **[date/time]**. No individual action was the sole cause; the event resulted from gaps in technical controls, consent governance, and detection coverage.

## Timeline

All times are **[time zone]**.

- **[Date/time]:** The malicious application was registered or first observed in the environment.
- **[Date/time]:** Initial user consent was granted following **[phishing or social-engineering method]**.
- **[Date/time]:** The application accessed **[resources/data]** using OAuth tokens.
- **[Date/time]:** Monitoring identified **[suspicious consent, API activity, or user report]**.
- **[Date/time]:** The security team began triage and confirmed unauthorized access.
- **[Date/time]:** New access by the application was blocked.
- **[Date/time]:** Existing grants, tokens, and relevant user sessions were revoked.
- **[Date/time]:** Affected accounts and data were reviewed; required notifications began.
- **[Date/time]:** Containment and remediation were completed.
- **[Date/time]:** Enhanced monitoring confirmed no further malicious activity.

## Root Cause

The attacker used a malicious OAuth application to persuade users to approve access to organizational resources. Because OAuth authorization can grant access without exposing or changing a user’s password, existing password-focused protections did not prevent the application from using valid tokens after consent was granted.

Contributing factors included:

- Users were permitted to consent to third-party applications with **[sensitive or broad]** permissions.
- The consent screen and application identity appeared sufficiently credible to avoid immediate suspicion.
- High-risk OAuth permissions did not consistently require administrator approval.
- Alerting for unusual application consent and token activity was incomplete or insufficiently prioritized.
- Existing guidance emphasized password phishing more than consent-based attacks.

## Impact

- **Affected users:** [number or range]
- **Affected systems:** [systems or services]
- **Data accessed:** [confirmed categories]
- **Data modified or deleted:** [none confirmed or description]
- **Duration of unauthorized access:** [duration]
- **External impact:** [customer, partner, regulatory, or operational impact]

The investigation **[found/did not find]** evidence that the attacker accessed **[specific data]**. Findings are based on currently available logs and may be updated if additional evidence becomes available.

## Remediation

Completed actions:

- Disabled and blocked the malicious OAuth application.
- Revoked all associated OAuth grants, access tokens, refresh tokens, and active sessions.
- Reviewed affected accounts for additional unauthorized applications and activity.
- Reset credentials where account compromise could not be excluded.
- Preserved relevant logs and indicators for investigation.
- Added detections for the application, associated infrastructure, and observed behaviors.
- Notified affected stakeholders in accordance with internal and external requirements.

Planned actions:

- Require administrator approval for applications requesting sensitive permissions.
- Restrict user consent to verified publishers and approved permission scopes.
- Establish recurring reviews of OAuth applications, grants, and service principals.
- Improve alerts for new application consent, unusual token use, and anomalous API access.
- Expand security education to cover OAuth consent phishing.
- Review logging coverage and retention for identity and cloud application activity.
- Define and test a response playbook for malicious OAuth applications.

## Lessons Learned

- Strong authentication controls do not, by themselves, prevent consent-based OAuth attacks.
- OAuth applications and grants must be governed as privileged access paths.
- Consent events require risk-based monitoring and timely review.
- Clearer permission descriptions and approval workflows can help users make safer decisions.
- Rapid coordination across security, identity, legal, privacy, and communications teams improved containment.
- Future exercises should include token theft and malicious application scenarios, not only password compromise.

# Internal Incident Post-Mortem: Malicious OAuth Application

## Incident Summary

On `[date]`, the Security team identified a malicious OAuth application that had been authorized by `[number]` users in the corporate identity environment. The application used deceptive consent prompts to obtain access to user account data and authentication tokens.

After validation, the application was disabled, its access grants were revoked, affected sessions and credentials were reset, and relevant indicators were blocked. The incident was contained on `[date/time]`. This document summarizes the event based on currently available evidence and is intended to improve organizational controls and response processes, not assign individual blame.

## Timeline

All times are in `[time zone]`.

| Date and time | Event |
|---|---|
| `[timestamp]` | Malicious OAuth application was registered or first observed in the environment. |
| `[timestamp]` | First known user authorized the application. |
| `[timestamp]` | The application began accessing authorized account data or tokens. |
| `[timestamp]` | Security monitoring generated an alert for `[unusual consent activity/suspicious API access/other indicator]`. |
| `[timestamp]` | Security Operations began triage and identified the OAuth application as malicious. |
| `[timestamp]` | New authorizations were blocked and the application was disabled. |
| `[timestamp]` | Existing OAuth grants and active sessions were revoked. |
| `[timestamp]` | Affected users were notified and required credential resets were initiated. |
| `[timestamp]` | Investigation established the known scope of affected users, data, and systems. |
| `[timestamp]` | Additional indicators and access restrictions were deployed. |
| `[timestamp]` | Incident was declared contained. |
| `[timestamp]` | Recovery and enhanced monitoring were completed. |

## Root Cause

The incident resulted from a malicious application successfully obtaining OAuth authorization from users through a deceptive consent flow. The application requested permissions that allowed it to access `[mail/files/profile/directory/other resources]` on users’ behalf.

Contributing factors included:

- Users were permitted to authorize third-party applications without prior administrative approval.
- The consent screen and application identity did not provide enough reliable information for users to distinguish the malicious application from a legitimate service.
- Requested OAuth permissions were broader than required for typical user-authorized applications.
- Alerting for unusual application consent and token use was incomplete or did not provide sufficient context for immediate escalation.
- Existing guidance emphasized password phishing more than OAuth consent abuse, which does not necessarily require disclosure of a password.
- Application inventory and periodic review processes did not identify the authorization before suspicious activity occurred.

No single action or individual caused the incident. The event was enabled by gaps across identity configuration, monitoring, application governance, and user-facing safeguards.

## Impact

The investigation identified:

- `[number]` users who authorized the malicious application.
- `[number]` accounts with confirmed or suspected unauthorized access.
- Potential exposure of `[email messages/files/contact information/profile data/other data]`.
- Unauthorized activity involving `[mailbox searches, message access, file downloads, forwarding rules, external sharing, or other actions]`.
- Service disruption associated with session revocation, credential resets, and temporary access restrictions.

At the time of this report, `[no evidence/evidence]` has been found of access to `[specific systems or data]`. Log retention and visibility limitations mean that `[describe any uncertainty]`. The investigation will be updated if additional evidence changes the assessed scope.

## Remediation

Completed actions:

- Disabled and blocked the malicious OAuth application.
- Revoked all associated consent grants, tokens, and active sessions.
- Reset credentials and authentication factors for affected accounts where appropriate.
- Removed unauthorized mailbox rules, delegated access, and external sharing configurations.
- Blocked identified domains, application identifiers, redirect URIs, IP addresses, and related indicators.
- Reviewed audit logs for additional affected users and suspicious application activity.
- Notified affected users, internal stakeholders, and `[legal/privacy/regulatory parties]` as required.
- Increased monitoring for related indicators and repeated authorization attempts.

Planned or in-progress actions:

- Require administrative approval for OAuth applications requesting sensitive permissions.
- Restrict user consent to verified publishers and low-risk permission sets.
- Implement automated alerts for new OAuth grants, high-risk permissions, unusual token use, and anomalous API access.
- Establish a recurring review of enterprise applications, publishers, permissions, and inactive grants.
- Apply least-privilege standards to approved OAuth integrations.
- Improve identity log retention and centralize OAuth consent and token telemetry.
- Update incident-response procedures to include OAuth application abuse and illicit consent scenarios.
- Provide focused awareness material explaining that account compromise can occur through application authorization without password disclosure.
- Test controls through periodic identity-security exercises.

## Lessons Learned

- OAuth consent is a security-sensitive action and should be governed similarly to software installation or privileged access.
- Password resets alone do not contain OAuth-based compromise; grants, refresh tokens, sessions, and application access must also be revoked.
- Effective detection requires visibility into both consent events and subsequent API behavior.
- Publisher verification and familiar branding reduce risk but should not replace permission controls and administrative review.
- Clear ownership of third-party application governance improves both prevention and response speed.
- Response procedures should explicitly address downstream changes such as mailbox rules, delegated permissions, and external file sharing.
- Timely coordination among Security, Identity, IT, Legal, Privacy, and Communications reduced the duration and potential impact of the incident.
- Controls should assume that well-designed deceptive prompts can mislead users and should minimize dependence on individual judgment.

On [date], the security team identified a malicious third-party OAuth application that had obtained access to [affected services/data] through authorization grants issued by [number] users. The application presented itself as [legitimate application or business purpose] and requested permissions that enabled it to access [mail, files, profile information, or other resources].

Upon confirmation, we disabled the application, revoked its OAuth grants and active sessions, blocked associated indicators, and initiated an investigation. This post-mortem reflects information available as of [date]. The investigation found [no evidence/evidence] that passwords were directly exposed; however, the stolen OAuth tokens allowed access without requiring users’ credentials or multi-factor authentication for each request.

## Timeline

All times are in [time zone].

- **[Date/time]:** The malicious application was registered or first observed in the environment.
- **[Date/time]:** The first affected user authorized the application.
- **[Date/time]:** The application began accessing [resources].
- **[Date/time]:** [Monitoring alert, user report, or external notification] identified suspicious OAuth activity.
- **[Date/time]:** Security began triage and confirmed unauthorized application access.
- **[Date/time]:** The application was disabled and blocked.
- **[Date/time]:** OAuth grants, refresh tokens, and affected user sessions were revoked.
- **[Date/time]:** Potentially affected users and internal stakeholders were notified.
- **[Date/time]:** Log review and impact analysis were completed.
- **[Date/time]:** Additional OAuth controls and monitoring were deployed.
- **[Date/time]:** The incident was closed, with longer-term remediation tracked separately.

## Root Cause

The incident was enabled by a combination of OAuth consent settings and social engineering. Users were permitted to authorize third-party applications without prior administrative review for the permissions requested. The malicious application used convincing branding and messaging to appear legitimate, leading affected users to approve access.

Multi-factor authentication reduced the risk of direct account takeover but did not prevent the incident because OAuth tokens granted after user consent can be used independently of the user’s password and subsequent authentication challenges.

Detection was delayed because existing monitoring focused primarily on password-based sign-ins and did not provide sufficient visibility into newly authorized applications, high-risk permission grants, or abnormal activity performed through OAuth tokens.

## Impact

- **Affected users:** [number or scope]
- **Affected systems:** [systems and services]
- **Permissions granted:** [permission scopes]
- **Data accessed:** [confirmed data types and date range]
- **Data modified or deleted:** [none identified/details]
- **External disclosure:** [none identified/details]
- **Operational impact:** [service disruption, response effort, or business impact]

The investigation identified [confirmed/suspected] access to [data or resources]. We found [no evidence/evidence] of direct password theft, persistence outside the OAuth grants, or access beyond the identified accounts. Because available logs [did/did not] provide complete historical coverage, [describe any residual uncertainty].

## Remediation

### Completed

- Disabled and blocked the malicious OAuth application.
- Revoked all associated consent grants, access tokens, and refresh tokens.
- Invalidated active sessions for affected users.
- Reviewed affected accounts for suspicious sign-ins, forwarding rules, delegated access, and other persistence mechanisms.
- Reset credentials where additional compromise could not be ruled out.
- Blocked identified domains, URLs, application identifiers, and related indicators.
- Preserved relevant logs and evidence.
- Notified affected users and appropriate internal stakeholders.

### Planned or In Progress

- Require administrative approval for applications requesting sensitive permissions.
- Restrict user consent to verified publishers and low-risk permission scopes.
- Establish a formal review process for new OAuth applications.
- Alert on newly authorized applications, unusual consent patterns, and high-risk scopes.
- Monitor token-based access separately from interactive sign-ins.
- Periodically review and remove unused applications and stale consent grants.
- Expand audit-log retention and centralize OAuth telemetry.
- Update security awareness material to address OAuth consent phishing.
- Conduct a follow-up review by [date] to verify remediation effectiveness.

## Lessons Learned

- OAuth consent is a distinct attack path from password theft and requires dedicated preventive and detective controls.
- Multi-factor authentication remains important but does not mitigate malicious applications that receive valid authorization grants.
- Application names, branding, and publisher claims are not sufficient indicators of legitimacy.
- Sensitive OAuth permissions should require review based on risk rather than relying solely on individual user judgment.
- Faster alerts for new applications and unusual token activity would have reduced the time between initial authorization and containment.
- Clear ownership of third-party application governance is necessary to ensure that consent policies, inventories, and reviews remain current.
- Response procedures should explicitly include revoking OAuth grants and refresh tokens, reviewing application-created persistence, and validating the scope of token-based access.

This incident resulted from gaps in controls and visibility rather than the actions of any single individual. The remediation work focuses on strengthening system-level safeguards so that similar attempts are prevented or detected earlier.
